description_full: Games Workshop Group PLC, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the design, manufacture, distribution, and sale of fantasy miniature figures and games in the United Kingdom, Continental Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand, Asia, and internationally. The company operates in two segments, Core and Licensing. It offers games under the Warhammer 40,000; Warhammer: The Horus Heresy; Warhammer: The Old World; Warhammer: Age of Sigmar; and Necromunda and Blood Bowl brand names, as well as has a licensed property for the Lord of the Rings. The company also publishes short stories, audio dramas, full length novels, and audio books under the Black Library name. In addition, it engages in the magazine newsstand business; and grants licences to third parties for the development of video games, PC games, media, and other products. The company sells its products through its own retail stores, third party independent retailers, and online stores. The company was incorporated in 1991 and is headquartered in Nottingham, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: Games Workshop Group is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $7.2B market cap on $881M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 89% against a 8% cost of capital — a 80-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 72% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $292M in free cash flow — roughly 33 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -13.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 5.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

news_headlines.title: Games Workshop Group (OTCMKTS:GMWKF) Stock Falls 4.3% – Here’s What Happened

sect: Its 42% operating margin runs 34pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 5.05x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 0.73, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $25K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 54% in the 2020 crash and 52% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $175 (margin of safety -25%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $129 to $243 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 26.2 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 24.3 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 24.8 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 9.2% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 89% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 80pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.20).
It runs a 72% gross margin and converts 33% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.30x, but high accruals (-13.2% of assets).
ROE of 61% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 16% last year, worth watching.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $169.5M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 29.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.1% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 22% of profits supports about 19.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 70%.
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (2.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 11 consecutive years.
people: With about 3,321 employees, each generates about $265K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $88K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (12x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
